$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-ϕ),
$$

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x=(R\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

$$

Here, ${\\color{blue}R}$ is the **amplitude** and ${\\color{red}\\phi}$ is the **phase** of the sine function.\n\nThe sum or difference of a sine function and a cosine function with the same argument can always be written as a sine function in amplitude-phase form. That is to say, if $a$ and $b$ are positive real numbers, then the expression\n\n$$\na \\sin x \\pm b \\cos x\n$$\n\ncan be written in the form \n\n$$\nR \\sin(x \\pm \\phi).\n$$\n\nfor some $R>0$ and $\\phi \\in \\left(0, \\dfrac{\\pi}{2}\\right).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "69964ee4-693c-5a43-af92-88232e3d1471" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2572 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "88224b15-9a6d-5755-a5b2-af292977df30" :step/math-academy-id 11889 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097469}} {:db/id 17592186097414 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097818 :tutorial/content "We've been using the amplitude-phase form for sine, but there is also an amplitude-phase form for cosine. If $a$ and $b$ are positive real numbers, then the expression\n\n$$\na \\cos x \\pm b \\sin x\n$$\n\ncan be written in the form \n\n$$\n{\\color{blue}R} \\cos(x \\mp {\\color{red}\\phi} )\n$$\n\nfor some ${\\color{blue}R}>0$ and ${\\color{red}\\phi} \\in \\left(0, \\dfrac{\\pi}{2}\\right).$ \n\nNote that the sign in the last formula flips due to the identity $\\cos(x \\mp \\phi) = \\cos x \\cos \\phi \\pm \\sin x \\sin \\phi,$ which reverses the sign when expanding.\n\nWriting this more explicitly, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}a\\operatorname{cos}x+b\\operatorname{sin}x & =R\\operatorname{cos}(x-ϕ) \\\\ a\\operatorname{cos}x-b\\operatorname{sin}x & =R\\operatorname{cos}(x+ϕ).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFor example, let's write the expression\n\n$$\n4\\sin{x}+\\cos{x}\n$$\n\nin amplitude-phase form with cosine. We start by expanding out the amplitude-phase form using the difference formula for cosine:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}R\\operatorname{cos}(x-ϕ) & =R(\\operatorname{cos}x\\operatorname{cos}ϕ+\\operatorname{sin}x\\operatorname{sin}ϕ) \\\\  & =R\\operatorname{cos}ϕ\\operatorname{cos}x+R\\operatorname{sin}ϕ\\operatorname{sin}x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we obtain the following equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4\\operatorname{sin}x+\\operatorname{cos}x & =R\\operatorname{cos}(x-ϕ) \\\\ 4\\operatorname{sin}x+\\operatorname{cos}x & =(R\\operatorname{sin}ϕ)\\operatorname{sin}x+(R\\operatorname{cos}ϕ)\\operatorname{cos}x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFirst, we find the phase $\\phi.$ Equating the coefficients of $\\sin x$ and $\\cos x,$ we have the following system:\n\n$$\n{\\begin{aligned}R\\operatorname{sin}ϕ=4 \\\\ R\\operatorname{cos}ϕ=1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nDividing the first equation by the second one, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{R\\operatorname{sin}ϕ}{R\\operatorname{cos}ϕ} & =\\frac{4}{1} \\\\ \\operatorname{tan}ϕ & =4 \\\\ ϕ & =\\operatorname{arctan}(4) \\\\  & \\approx 1.326\\,\\text{rad}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to three decimal places.\n\nNow, we find the amplitude $R.$ Squaring the first and the second equations of the system and adding the results together, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{(R\\operatorname{sin}ϕ)}^{2}+{(R\\operatorname{cos}ϕ)}^{2} & ={4}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\\\ {R}^{2}({sin}^{2}ϕ+{cos}^{2}ϕ) & =16+1 \\\\ {R}^{2} & =17 \\\\ R & =\\sqrt{17}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that we only considered the positive root, since $R>0.$\n\nFinally, we can write the initial expression in amplitude-phase form as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4\\operatorname{sin}x+\\operatorname{cos}x & =\\sqrt{17}\\operatorname{cos}(x-\\operatorname{arctan}(4)) \\\\  & \\approx
